text:
Sailing home from Troy, Odysseus lands in the country of the Cyclopes.

Book Nine never says where, because Homer cares about what happens next, not about a map.

He picks twelve men, takes a goatskin of wine, and walks up to a cave.

Inside, the racks are heavy with cheese, the pens are crowded with lambs, and nobody is home.

The crew beg him to take the cheeses and run.

But Odysseus wants to meet the owner, and he hopes the owner will give him a present. but Odysseus is famous for being clever, not sensible.

It is the first of many decisions his men will regret.

At dusk the owner comes home, and he looks less like a man than a wooded mountain peak standing alone.

The men press back into the shadows and hold their breath.

He drives the flock inside and rolls a stone across the door.

Homer says twenty-two wagons could not have moved it.

He asks the strangers who they are, and whether they are traders or pirates.

Odysseus asks for hospitality in the name of Zeus, who protects guests.

The giant answers that Cyclopes do not care about Zeus.

They keep no laws and hold no assemblies, and they think themselves stronger than the gods.

The men are shut in with a creature who fears nothing.

The only way out is behind a stone no human can lift.
